title: Between two (Avot 3:2)
hookLine: when two sit together and words of Torah pass between them, the Presence rests with them
tomorrow: what turns a pizza night into something holy?

cards: Two people on a couch, one script between them, running the same scene for the ninth time. Yesterday's riddle asked who else shows up when two friends share a line.
Rabbi Chananiah ben Teradion answers in Avot: two who sit with no words of Torah between them, that's a seat of scorners, a phrase from the first psalm.
But two who sit, and words of Torah pass between them, the Shechinah, the Presence, rests between them. That's who shows up. Now the argument starts: what should those words sound like?

teach.h: ONE SIDE: ONE TO ANOTHER, GENTLY.
teach.b: One side says: listen to the verse the Mishnah brings. Malachi writes, "Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it." One to another.
Conversation, not combat. On this view the Presence rests where people speak gently, take turns, and listen as much as they talk. A pair that shouts has lost the thread.
The other side says: you've never watched a chavruta, a study pair, at work.

teach.h: THE OTHER: LIKE ENEMIES, THEN FRIENDS.
teach.b: The Talmud says that a father and son, or a teacher and student, studying Torah together can become like enemies to each other, and they don't leave the spot until they've become friends who love each other.
On this view the Presence doesn't flinch at a raised voice; argument is how two people take a text seriously.
Each side has something the other needs. The gentle reading guards against cruelty dressed up as rigor. The fierce reading guards against politeness that never really engages.
And notice what both keep: two people who stay at the table. The scorners' seat isn't the loud one.
It's the one where nothing worth saying passes between them at all.

how: In yeshivas and study halls, students learn in pairs called chavruta, reading a text aloud together and debating its meaning.

o: the gap between what a text says and what it means
the space between two who share Torah, where the Presence rests
a rule that study must happen with exactly two people

games.q: two ways to sit — tap the pairs.
p: they spake often one to another

s: the Mishnah calls two people sitting with no words of Torah a 'seat of scorners'
it borrows the phrase from the first psalm.
in Avot, the Presence rests only inside a synagogue
it rests between two who share words of Torah, wherever they sit.
the Talmud pictures partners arguing like enemies until they love each other.

games.q: your study partner says real learning should always be calm and polite. what's the best case for the other side?
o: partners can argue like enemies and still leave loving each other.
arguing proves you studied harder, so the louder one wins.
calm study doesn't count; the Mishnah requires a fight.
games.why: the Talmud pictures study partners who become like enemies and don't leave until they love each other. Malachi's picture is quieter. the tradition keeps both.

practice: Choose one person you could share a line with: Akavia's three questions, or the fish with no ruler. Write it to them in a sentence or two of your own words, and send it now or save it for the right moment.
Then sit with the thought that a line between two people is, in the Mishnah's words, a place the Presence can rest.

wordCard.voice: Between two: the space between people who share words of Torah, where, Avot says, the Shechinah rests.

orig.note: Hebrew: the Presence, God's nearness, which Avot 3:2 says rests between two who study.

carryVoice: Keep this: the presence rests between, whether the pair speaks gently or argues to the end. That's the day.

sources.ref: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:2 (Rabbi Chananiah ben Teradion: two who sit together)

sources.q: Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 30b (study partners become like enemies, and do not leave until they love each other)
